entities.name: Richard I of Capua
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard Drengot, a pivotal figure in the Norman conquest of Southern Italy, rose from Count of Aversa (1049–1078) to become Prince of Capua and Duke of Gaeta (1064–1078), establishing a powerful independent principality. His career, marked by relentless military expansion and astute diplomacy, significantly shaped the political landscape of the Italian peninsula during the mid-11th century. Operating amidst the fragmentation of Lombard and Byzantine power, Richard, alongside his more famous contemporary Robert Guiscard, played a crucial role in consolidating Norman rule and challenging both imperial and papal authority, fundamentally altering the region's trajectory.

His reign was characterized by aggressive territorial acquisition and strategic maneuvering against powerful adversaries. Richard famously participated in the Battle of Civitate in 1053, a decisive Norman victory over a combined papal and imperial force, which forced Pope Leo IX to recognize Norman legitimacy. He then systematically expanded his domains, culminating in the siege and capture of Capua in 1058, a major Lombard stronghold, followed by the acquisition of Gaeta. His most audacious act was the siege of Rome in 1066, a demonstration of Norman military might that compelled Pope Alexander II to acknowledge his titles and possessions in exchange for protection, effectively making him a papal vassal.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Richard I of Capua was a key architect of Norman power in Southern Italy, expanding his principality through military conquest and challenging both papal and imperial authority. His actions directly contributed to the political landscape that would eventually form the Kingdom of Sicily.
